# Abolition of slavery (`abolition_of_slavery`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by human_equality_dignity, natural_rights, free_press, representative_government
- Core idea: No human being can be owned, bought or sold. Abolition took different paths. Some jurisdictions freed people immediately; others first banned the trade or freed children born after a specified date. Ending ownership in practice required enforcement and protection against forced labour under a different name. The arguments that moved people were the testimony of the enslaved, the plain moral claim that what you would not suffer you may not inflict, and the observation that free workers who gain from their effort work better than whipped ones. Freed people need land or wages, or they fall into debt bondage.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming emancipation on paper secures freedom: owners could retain control through coercive labour contracts, policing and debt
  - Forgetting compensation and enforcement: Britain paid owners 20 million pounds (about 40 % of a year's budget) and kept a naval squadron off West Africa for decades
  - Freeing people with nothing: without land, tools or wages, sharecropping, 'apprenticeship' and debt peonage follow
  - Assuming slavery was dying on its own because it was unprofitable: plantation slavery was profitable until abolished
  - Reading the Cyrus Cylinder as abolishing slavery: it presents the king as a restorer of cults and communities after his conquest of Babylon
- History: mesopotamia: law codes regulate slavery and debt bondage; royal debt-release edicts (from c. 2400 BC) free debt slaves but not chattel slaves; greece: 4th c. BC – Alcidamas: 'God has left all men free; nature has made no one a slave' (quoted in a scholion on Aristotle's Rhetoric); no practical consequence; rome: 1st c. AD – Stoics such as Seneca (Letter 47) urge humane treatment; c. 379 Gregory of Nyssa condemns owning slaves outright in a sermon; the institution continues; china: AD 9 – Wang Mang forbids the buying and selling of slaves, repealed AD 12; 1720s the Yongzheng emperor frees several hereditary 'mean' status groups; legal abolition 1910; east_asia: 1590 – Hideyoshi bans the slave trade in Japan; Korea frees government slaves in 1801 and abolishes hereditary slave status in 1886–1894; india: c. 250 BC – Ashoka's edicts enjoin proper treatment of slaves and servants; 1843 Indian Slavery Act withdraws legal recognition; islamic: 7th c. – the Quran commends freeing slaves and the law forbids enslaving free Muslims, without abolition; 1846 Tunisia abolishes slavery; 1847–1857 Ottoman bans on the slave trade; 1962 Saudi Arabia; europe: 1256 – Bologna buys the freedom of nearly 6,000 serfs (Liber Paradisus); 1772 Somerset case in England; 1794 France abolishes (restored 1802, final 1848); 1807 British slave trade ban; 1833 British emancipation act; 1861 Russian serfs freed; americas: 1542 – Spanish New Laws forbid enslaving Indians, weakly enforced; 1777 Vermont; 1780 Pennsylvania's gradual abolition; 1791–1804 Haitian Revolution, the only slave revolt to found a state; 1865 United States; 1888 Brazil; africa: 1807 onwards – suppression of the Atlantic trade; 1981 Mauritania, the last state to abolish slavery in law
- Read:
  - Seymour Drescher, Abolition: A History of Slavery and Antislavery (2009)
  - Adam Hochschild, Bury the Chains (2005)
  - Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789)
